New Yorkers pay some of the highest commercial health insurance premiums in the country. My proposal would preserve all federally required essential health benefits while allowing New Yorkers to choose eligible additional state-mandated coverage based on their individual needs and stage of life. [image: HOW MANY MORE INNOCENT NEW YORKERS HAVE TO DIE? In 2019, Albany passed sweeping bail reform legislation that took effect January 1, 2020. On February 13, 2022, Christina Yuna Lee was followed into her Manhattan apartment, sexually assaulted and stabbed more than 40 times by Assamad Nash, a repeat offender who was on supervised release in THREE other criminal cases. He was later sentenced to 30 years to life. Liz Krueger has spent 24 years in Albany and continues to oppose meaningful changes to New York’s bail reform laws. Even after horrific crimes like Christina’s murder, Krueger has publicly defended the state’s approach to bail reform. Meanwhile, New Yorkers are left questioning why repeat offenders remain on our streets. How many more victims? How many more grieving families? When will Albany put public safety first? I support restoring judicial discretion, strengthening accountability for violent repeat offenders, and reforming laws that fail to protect innocent New Yorkers. On November 3rd, it’s time to break up with Liz Krueger. How many more innocent victims have to die while she and others refuse to change their failed bail reform policies? END THE NEGLECT. [image: IN THE NEWS | My Interview with Patch What does being a Republican really mean in today’s political climate? Does it mean blindly supporting the Trump administration? And what makes someone who’s never held political office qualified to represent New Yorkers? In my latest interview with Patch, I answer these questions candidly, including where I agree and disagree with my own party, my views on immigration and healthcare, and why I believe good policy should never be dictated by party loyalty. I also share what sets me apart from career politicians. I’ve been an immigrant, a renter, a homeowner, a mother, an employee, an entrepreneur, insured and uninsured. I’ve experienced government assistance and navigated government systems that have failed me. I’ve lived many of the challenges that politicians spend their careers debating. I never intended to enter politics. But I believe those experiences give me a perspective that is often missing in Albany. My goal isn’t a political career. It’s to turn real-life experience into meaningful legislative change. Thank you to Patch for the opportunity to share my story, my independence, and the policies I intend to pursue. [image: IT’S TIME FOR A BREAKUP. 24 YEARS IS LONG ENOUGH! The first step toward restoring public safety in New York is fixing our broken bail reform laws. As a candidate for State Senate, I fully support this mission, and as a state legislator, I will fight to make these long-overdue changes. @sarithaforny , candidate for Attorney General, and I share the same commitment to public safety. This election gives New Yorkers an opportunity to replace longtime incumbents like Liz Krueger and Letitia James with leaders who will put the safety of innocent people first. According to the NYPD, the number of individuals arrested three or more times for felony assault has increased by 205.6% since 2018. In May, 76-year-old retired teacher Ross Falzone died after being pushed down subway stairs. The man charged with his murder had four prior arrests that year and had been released from psychiatric evaluation just hours earlier. This is just one of numerous tragedies raising serious concerns about repeat violent offenders. Not every victim dies. [image: It’s time for a breakup. 24 years is enough, and it’s time to stop the rise in crime. In 2019, Albany passed sweeping bail reform, eliminating cash bail for most misdemeanors and nonviolent felonies. When Governor Hochul pushed for changes in 2022 amid rising concerns about public safety, my opponent Liz Krueger defended the law and argued that rising crime was not caused by bail reform. Six years later, New Yorkers are still living with the consequences of policies that make it harder to keep repeat offenders off our streets. I’m running to amend the law, restore greater judicial discretion and give judges the ability to consider public safety and repeat offenses when making pretrial decisions. Manhattan deserves laws that protect the rights of the accused and the safety of the public. After 24 years with the same representation it's enough, let's end the Neglect. [image: I’m honored to have been invited to present at Weill Cornell Medicine’s David Rogers Health Policy Colloquium. Healthcare has always been close to my heart. I spent 15 years in the industry, working with physicians and hospital systems and training doctors. I saw firsthand how bureaucracy and policy can make it harder for physicians to practice medicine and ultimately impact the care patients receive. Now, two of my worlds are colliding: healthcare and public policy. I’m especially excited to speak with the next generation of physicians about how healthcare policy becomes law and how clinicians can help shape it. Doctors on the front lines see what works and what doesn’t, and their voices should have a meaningful path into policymaking. As a State Senator, I would work to make sure those voices are heard in Albany and that good ideas can move through the right channels to become better policy.
